concept.name: Rounding bottom
concept.definition: A long-term bullish reversal pattern in which a decline gradually flattens into a shallow U- or bowl-shaped low and then curves back upward, best seen on weekly charts. It represents a slow transfer from distribution to accumulation — sentiment shifting from bearish to bullish at a steady pace — and is confirmed when price breaks above the reaction high at the start of the pattern. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Instead of a violent V-shaped reversal, selling pressure fades week by week and buying interest returns just as gradually, tracing a bowl — patient accumulation replacing capitulation.
concept.mechanics: The decline into the low and the advance out of it should take roughly comparable time; the low should be rounded over weeks, not a sharp spike. Ideally volume also traces a saucer: high during the initial decline, minimal through the flat middle, rising on the advance. Confirmation is a breakout above the pattern's left-edge reaction high with volume expansion; duration (months to years) indicates significance.
concept.failure_modes: Because it forms over months, the pattern invites countless premature calls — most 'rounding bottoms' in progress are just flat, trendless drift that eventually resolves downward. A 'broken saucer' (price spiraling away before completing the bowl) is a recognized failure variant.
concept.misconceptions: That there is a reliable measured price target — conventionally there is none, though some analysts project the depth of the U. Also that the two sides must be symmetrical; capturing the gradual sentiment shift matters more than geometric perfection.
concept.example: A stock declines from $17 to $11.22 over months, bases in a flat saucer near $12, then advances with steadily rising volume and breaks above the $17 left-edge high — confirming the long-term reversal.

citations.source: The Economic Times, ET Wealth: Why rounding bottoms & tops formations are more predictable and reliable than V-shaped formations
